entries.title: Sky to bring back coach Tyler Marsh for third season
entries.summary: <p>Tyler Marsh has new life.</p><p>Just a week ago he was reckoning with his future in Chicago after another season failed to live up to expectations. He told reporters that whether or not he was back leading the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> in 2027, he was grateful for his experience — and that he if he was back, he'd approach it with the same zeal he always has. </p><p>Now he can rest easy. The Sky front office wants to see what the third-year coach can do, confirming that he’ll be returning next season.</p><p>“It was going to be incredibly unfair to judge someone that has yet to play with healthy rosters as a young coach,” general manager Jeff Pagliocca said in his exit interview on Thursday.</p><p>Marsh’s luck hasn’t been great since joining the Sky as a first-time head coach in 2025. In each year one of his top players tore their ACL — Courtney Vandersloot in 2025 and Rickea Jackson in 2026. This season he also started the year without Vandersloot and Azura Stevens, and ultimately lost point guard Skylar Diggins to injury 19 games in.</p><p>Still, midway through the season, Pagliocca told the Sun-Times that even despite the injuries across their starting lineup, he expected the team to make the playoffs. The Sky finished well short in 11th place, and blowing close games was a big reason why.</p><p>Pagliocca said Thursday that he saw enough growth from Marsh to give him confidence. </p><p>“I never heard him make excuses," Pagliocca said of Marsh. "I never heard him shy away from taking responsibility, in a lot of moments where he didn’t need to or shouldn’t have. We were in those games. Whether the players weren't executing or he wasn’t executing, he was owning that responsibility.</p><p>"He’s as selfless as I’ve been around. He coaches for the right reasons. He kept the locker room intact.</p><p>“He knows what he wants to do differently, and he’s made me believe that he’s the guy to lead this team."</p>

region</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjkihky-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Lisa Shames</a></h5><p>It's apple picking season in the Midwest, and we've got a list of some orchards in the area worth the trek.</p><p>Corn mazes, cider doughnuts, petting zoos and plenty of u-pick apples (plus, sunflowers, raspberries and pumpkins in some cases) await at these farms in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin. They've also got a maze made from cedar planks, antique John Deere tractors, wagon tours of the property and more.</p><p>Kuipers Family Farm, Maple Park<br>In addition to apple picking, they've got a pumpkin picking farm, live music on the weekends, pig races, a "farmyard bar" and more.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjkihky-l-il/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What makes Chicago sports fans unlike others?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: CATCH-22: Mike Martz thinks Bears 'finally got it right' with coach, QB
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p><b>Mike Martz (1), </b>who was watching Monday Night Football back home in St. Louis when he recognized a play from his past: The Sucker Sneak.</p><p>“It just tickled me,” Martz told me on Tuesday.</p><p>Bears quarterback<b> Case Keenum</b> <b>(2)</b> was under center on third-and-goal from the Eagles’ 1 halfway through the fourth quarter. When he took the snap, the Bears’ guards pulled — left guard <b>Joe Thuney (3)</b> to his left and right guard <b>Jonah Jackson</b> <b>(4)</b> to his right. Defensive tackles <b>Jordan Davis</b> <b>(5)</b> and <b>Byron Young</b> <b>(6)</b> did what they’re coached to do when the guards in front of them pull — charge forward.</p><p>When they did, Keenum simply pushed ahead behind the uncovered center for an easy one-yard touchdown.</p><p>It’s a Jedi mind trick of a play.</p><p>“You can’t undo good coaching, so you take advantage of it,” said Martz, the architect of the Greatest Show on Turf Rams. “Those guys are going to jet charge — they’re going to get up the field as fast as they can. They’re trying to penetrate and knock things back.</p><p>“You just let them do that. You don’t even have to block them.”</p><p>Martz shared cutups of his sneak with the Dolphins when <b>Ben Johnson (7)</b> coached there, though he’s unsure if Johnson had already seen it.</p><p>Believing in the play takes faith, but Keenum said “my word of the week was ‘trust.’”</p><p>Few have ever run it in a game. Martz called the play for a 2-yard <b>Kurt Warner</b> <b>(8)</b> touchdown in the Super Bowl 24 years ago. Two years later, <b>Marc Bulger (9)</b>, another Rams quarterback, ran the sneak for 15 yards. The 49ers pulled it off in 2024.</p><p>“It’s never not worked, to be honest with you,” Martz said.</p><p>The fact Johnson ran the sneak against a team known for the brute-force “Tush Push” wasn’t lost on Martz.</p><p>“I get such a kick out of that,” said Martz, who texted Johnson after he ran the play. “Only Ben would do that.”</p><h3><b>The better Bears scrambler, of course, is …</b></h3><p><b>Caleb Williams (10), </b>who remains sidelined with a pulled hamstring. Martz thinks he and Johnson make a perfect pairing.</p><p>“Chicago, my gosh, they’re so lucky to have [Johnson],” he said. “He’s going to be there a long time and be a great coach. They finally got it right. They got the quarterback right, too. Caleb, he was lost in the wilderness until Ben got him.”</p><p>Players who have had success off-script often find it hard at first to conform to a strict offensive system. Martz had a similar experience with <b>Jay Cutler (11)</b> when he was the Bears’ offensive coordinator from 2011-12.</p><p>Williams had to “unlearn” everything from his rookie year, Martz said. With Johnson, Williams has a ridiculously high ceiling.</p><p>“He doesn’t know how good he can be,” he said.</p><p>Martz has been enamored by Johnson since his stint as the Lions’ play-caller.</p><p>“I knew he was different,” Martz said. “It’s not just the play selection, which is impeccable. …</p><p>“The great play-callers? When you get into the game and they’re taking something away, you can morph into something else. He can do that. You’ve got to carry a pretty good plan to do that.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Keenum reminded Martz of his own former QBs …</b></h3><p>“<b>Trent Green (12),</b> <b>Kurt Warner (13), Jon Kitna (14)</b>, <b>Bulger</b> … They had something to prove,” Martz said. “When you have a guy with talent like that that has something to prove, they tend to play pretty good.”</p><p>Keenum seems to be the same way.</p><p>“Guys that I like coaching the best are the guys that have been kicked around a little bit,” Martz said.</p><p></p><h3><b>It’ll help him become a football player …</b></h3><p><b>Kyler Keenum (15), </b>Case’s son<b>, </b>was born<b> </b>in Virginia while his dad played for the Commanders in 2019. Case had his parents scoop dirt from his Texas backyard and put it in a mason jar, which Case slipped under the delivery table so Kyle could be “born on Texas soil.”</p><p>That might help his future NFL career. Texas boasts the most native NFL players — both active and all-time — as well as the most Hall of Famers. Across NFL history, Texans have played more games and scored more touchdowns than players from any other state.</p><p>The Bears boast four Texas-born Hall of Famers — <b>Ed Sprinkle</b> <b>(16)</b> of Bradshaw, <b>Bulldog Turner (17) </b>of Plains and <b>Steve McMichael (18)</b> and <b>Mike Singletary (19)</b> of Houston.</p><h3><b>Speaking of backup QBs …</b></h3><p><b>Trevor Siemian (20)</b> played quarterback the last time the Bears faced the Jets. <b>Justin Fields’ (21)</b> backup strained his oblique while warming up at The Meadowlands in 2022, thouh, prompting the Bears to name <b>Nathan Peterman</b> <b>(22)</b> the starter.</p><p>The medication Siemian took kicked in before the game began, though, and the team then named him the starter a second time before kickoff.</p><p>The Bears then lost 31-10 to a Jets team that went on to lose the next six games.</p>

He went 32-for-60 for 354 yards, three interceptions and a 61.4 passer rating. The year: 1997.<b>Season</b>: 1-2.</p><p></p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><p></p><p><b>Bears, 27-16:</b> This is a must-have game for the Bears, and getting to 3-1 in Caleb Williams’ absence is huge. <b>Season:</b> 1-2.</p><p></p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p></p><p><b>Bears, 31-18: </b>A team that’s 1-2 and still considered on the positive side of “surprising” can be more “scary" than anything. This Aaron Glenn/Ben Johnson reunion won’t take the Bears by surprise. <b>Season: </b>1-2.</p><p></p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p></p><p><b>Bears, 24-20:</b> Yes, the Bears should beat the Jets. And then run it some more. <b>Season</b>: 1-2.</p><p></p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p></p><p><b>Bears, 28-14:</b> Through three games, we’ve learned a couple of things: Johnson can turn any quarterback, young and old, into a world-beater, and I’m the kind of prognosticator whose picks you go against. By that logic, you should be filthy rich! I’m just filthy. <b>Season: </b>0-3.</p>

entries.title: Renee Good's family sues U.S., immigration officials over her killing in Minneapolis
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Macklin Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal deportation campaign in Minneapolis.</p><p>The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee's brother Brent Ganger.</p><p>The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment.</p><h3>Officer shot Good as she turned her car away from him</h3><p>Good was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minneapolis-ice-immigration-renee-good-shooting-3f2a9e26ddac9455b931fecee5989d18" target="_blank" >Bystander video shows</a> Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.</p><p>Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the SUV. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer orders again, “Get out of the car.”</p><p>Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”</p><p>One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Good, according to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/immigration-minnesota-ice-shooting-protest-cad39aa94829e1e11468e3e345af2826" target="_blank" >an analysis of the videos</a> by The Associated Press and others.</p><p>Federal officials at the time said the officer <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minnesota-immigration-enforcement-crackdown-woman-shot-5158ce0838305b491c95db97b970cd03" target="_blank" >acted in self-defense</a> and that Good had engaged in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/vance-minnesota-immigration-enforcement-06b23b428edcc8498362be4ac656f201" target="_blank" >“an act of domestic terrorism.”</a></p><h3>One lawsuit alleges wrongful death</h3><p>The lawsuit against the U.S. seeks damages for Good's wrongful death and “the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” according to a news release by lawyers for Ganger and Becca Good.</p><p>The lawsuit, which seeks a bench trial, also alleges “intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress” on Becca Good.</p><p>Becca and Good, the mother of three children, were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently moved to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.</p><h3>Another lawsuit alleges conspiracy to conceal evidence</h3><p>The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial. It claims the federal government moved to hide evidence of what happened Jan. 7.</p><p>The lawsuit states the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, “were the predictable and intended product of the operation.”</p><p>It describes a “carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign.”</p><p>The lawsuit names Ross as a defendant, as well as: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; Corey Lewandowski, a campaign manager for President Donald Trump who also served as one of Noem's advisers; White House border czar Tom Homan; former acting director of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.</p><h3>Good’s partner acknowledges other lives lost in deportation campaign</h3><p>The killing of Good and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minneapolis-ice-fbi-alex-pretti-immigration-65a963816603a08bbc9db83961dd173f" target="_blank" >another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti</a>, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/minneapolis-shootings-kristi-noem-ice-congress-add9ac7b90f5677621009e8a603c0141" target="_blank" >calls to rein in</a> immigration enforcement. At least 10 people <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/immigration-enforcement-deaths-eight-houston-35b6d6f9b9715edd064009e195547b2b" target="_blank" >have died</a> in encounters with immigration officers during Trump’s second term.</p><p>In social media accounts, Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.</p><p>In an interview shortly after her death, Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”</p><p>Good's partner noted the broader loss to communities nationwide.</p><p>“As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times,” Becca Good said in a news release Thursday. “So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones. To everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family.”</p>

entries.title: Boy, 15, fourth suspect charged with murder of man pushed off moving Red Line train
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy is the fourth suspect charged with the murder of Kyle Bickham who was pushed off of a moving Red Line train last month. </p><p>The boy, who isn’t named because he's a minor, was arrested Tuesday and charged with first-degree murder, one count of aggravated battery of a transit employee and one count of mob action, Chicago police said.</p><p>Police did not release court information for the boy. </p><p>The charges come after Christian S. McBounds, 18, 19-year-old Katlar Parchman and a 15-year-old girl have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/23/third-person-of-interest-being-questioned-in-murder-of-man-pushed-from-moving-red-line-train" target="_blank" >already been charged with murder</a>. </p><p>Bickham, 29, was pushed off of a moving train Sept. 7 near the 69th Street Red Line station after a fight broke out between him and Parchman, officials said. </p><p>Bickham and the teen girl started arguing, and at one point, Bickham allegedly spit at the girl and hit Parchman, according to CTA surveillance footage reviewed by prosecutors. Soon after, all four attackers started repeatedly punching Bickham. One of the males choked him, while the other male pulled the emergency lever for one of the train’s sliding doors as it was moving.</p><p>The 15-year-old girl grabbed Bickham by his head and shoulders, and with the help of one of the males,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/12/family-calls-for-cta-security-upgrades-after-man-was-fatally-thrown-from-moving-cta-train" target="_blank" > threw him off the moving train</a>, according to prosecutors. Bickham was hit by a train traveling in the other direction.</p><p>The death <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/07/labor-day-weekend-shooting" target="_blank" >was the ninth homicide</a> of the long Labor Day holiday weekend. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/07/cfd-1-dead-on-cta-red-line-tracks-near-63rd-street" target="_blank" >Police originally reported</a> a person had jumped from the train.<br></p>

entries.title: Northwestern's big night at the new Ryan Field is here. Will an upset of Penn State come with it?
entries.summary: <p>Here’s the thing about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/07/21/northwestern-football-new-ryan-field-stadium-review" target="_blank" >Northwestern’s new Ryan Field</a> that stands out the most, aside from the gaudy $875 million price tag and the still-very-real question of whether or not even a spectacular football stadium will make die-hard <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Wildcats</a> fans out of a larger slice of the local sports-fan populace:</p><p>Holy mother of purple, are the paying customers (not to mention the 3,000-plus undergraduates getting into games for no extra charge on top of the wheelbarrows of gold required to attend the school) ever going to be right on top of the action.</p><p><b>Penn State (-3) at Northwestern </b>(7 p.m. Friday, Fox 32 ,720-AM) is what we in the business like to call a football matchup, and a good one at that. But the details of what unfolds in between the lines will be a secondary story to the spectacle of opening night in the new digs, which happens to come on the 100th anniversary of the inauguration of the old joint.</p><p>Dyche Stadium, later renamed Ryan Field, was the worst stadium in the Big Ten, and that might be one of the kindest things one could say about it.</p><p>Oh, how different this is going to be.</p><p>“I would say it’s the best stadium in the world,” coach David Braun said this week.</p><p>The key to the whole operation, again, is going to be the proximity of fans to the field in a venue that seats only 35,000 but is designed to get extra-loud. From the nearest seats, the sideline will be a mere 48 feet away. From the farthest ones, the sideline will be 136 feet away. If you’re having trouble picturing what that looks like, just consider this — at Michigan Stadium, the mother of all football colossuses with a capacity of over 107,000, the nearest or best seats are 235 feet from the sideline.</p><p>You want to kiss a ref? This might be your best shot.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/IkBfenLZXQ8?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Ryan Field - Northwestern University Wildcats Stadium Completion | September 2026 - drone footage"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Wildcats fans should have a real chance to impact games, even if for some of them it means having to learn to go a little crazier on Saturdays than they’re accustomed to.</p><p>“Let’s go,” Braun said. “Let’s turn this into the best home-field advantage in college football.”</p><p>Now, can we talk about the game itself just a little?</p><p>If you watched the Wildcats throttle Colorado 41-7 in the final game at the lakefront pop-up venue and then go to defending national champ Indiana and hang in there in a 29-23 defeat, you’ve realized by now this is a good team. You’ve noted the poise, skill and overall excellent play of transfer quarterback Aidan Chiles and the fact he has one of the Big Ten’s best targets in Griffin Wilde. You’ve seen safety Robert Fitzgerald and linebacker Kobe McKinzie tackle everything that isn’t nailed down.</p><p>And you’ve come to accept that Braun — a virtual unknown when he took over for Pat Fitzgerald in 2023 amid a hazing scandal — has been a more-than-able replacement. These days, he and White Sox general manager Chris Getz, who is succeeding despite his own 2023 appointment having been widely panned, remind me of each other. In my imagination, they’ll gather soon enough over a couple of cold ones as long-lost friends. Or not. Somebody rein me in here.</p><p>Penn State blew a 17-point lead and lost to Wisconsin last week at Beaver Stadium, which seats over 106,000 and ranks right behind Michigan Stadium in that category. The Nittany Lions have a formidable QB-receiver combo themselves in Rocco Becht and Kobe Howard, a strong running game and, of course, a brand name that can never be overlooked. If there were a classic Penn State pass rush to go with it, the collapse against Wisconsin and ensuing tumble out of the Top 25 wouldn’t have happened.</p><p>But here comes another idle thought: Maybe Northwestern can let the Bears’ bigwigs run around on the field at halftime just for a little new-stadium inspiration?</p><p>I’m picking a Wildcats upset, 23-21. Some kind of night, that’ll make it.</p><p><b>OTHER WEEK 3 PICKS</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday.</i></p><p><b>No. 3 Notre Dame (-21½) at North Carolina </b>(11 a.m., ESPN, 780-AM): If not for a seemingly endless weather delay that sabotaged North Carolina at Clemson, the Tar Heels would be 3-0, media would be buzzing about Bill Belichick and there’s no way the spread would be this huge. Yeah, well. Irish, 34-17.</p><p><b>No. 5 Ohio State (-14½) at No. 14 Iowa </b>(2:30 p.m., CBS 2): No, Iowa isn’t going to win at Michigan and shock the mighty Buckeyes back-to-back. Just stop already. OSU, 27-16.</p><p><b>No. 8 Florida (-5½) at No. 25 Missouri </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): There’s being good again, and then there’s being good enough to consistently win SEC games on the road again. Are the Gators really there yet? Tigers by a field goal.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 7 Alabama (-5½) at No. 16 Mississippi State </b>(11 a.m., ABC 7): The whole world is talking about Bulldogs QB Kamario Taylor, who has been electric. Do you know how many times in the last 12 years MSU has won a game in which both teams were ranked, though? Try once. OK, so it was last week against Missouri, but still. Rammer Jammer, I’ve got Bammer by a touchdown.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>Purdue (+10½) at Illinois </b>(3:15 p.m., BTN): Have the Boilermakers considered playing their home games in Champaign? They won seven in a row at Memorial Stadium before losing in overtime there in 2024. Some rivalries are just weird like that. Illini win but fail to cover.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>7-1 straight-up, 4-4 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>22-8 straight-up, 13-17 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/07/21/northwestern-football-new-ryan-field-stadium-review" >New Ryan Field gives Northwestern a spectacular football venue 100 years in the making</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/02/03/northwestern-new-ryan-field-delay" target="_blank" >Northwestern’s new Ryan Field won’t open until Oct. 2 against Penn State: exclusive</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mariachi Herencia de México está teniendo su momento luego de tocar el himno nacional estadounidense
entries.summary: <p>El mariscal de campo de los Chicago Bears, Case Keenum, no es el único que está disfrutando del brillo de una actuación magnífica durante el juego de Monday Night Football.</p><p>El Mariachi Herencia de México, nominado al Grammy, se volvió viral por su presentación antes del juego de fútbol americano el lunes por la noche, acumulando millones de vistas en internet y desatando una fiebre mediática.</p><p>“No he dormido mucho”, dijo el martes César Maldonado, fundador del grupo de 14 integrantes, en DreamCatcher Cafe del vecindario Back of the Yards. “Ha sido una locura mediática. Hemos estado haciendo entrevistas todo el día, pero ha sido una energía positiva increíble para todos”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d40000" name="module-d40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El mariachi, vestido con trajes de mariachi azules y moños con los colores y el logotipo de los Bears, interpretó una versión del “Star-Spangled Banner” inspirada en el trompetista de jazz cubanoestadounidense, Arturo Sandoval, marcando la primera vez que una banda de mariachi tocó el himno nacional en la historia de los Chicago Bears.</p><p>Con sede en Chicago, el mariachi fue invitado a interpretar el himno nacional como parte de la celebración del Mes de la Herencia Hispana de los Bears. Hace dos años, el grupo se presentó en el medio tiempo de un partido de los Bears en casa, lo que llevó a esta más reciente invitación.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="es" dir="ltr">The Mariachi Herencia de México performed the national anthem in Chicago 🎶 <a href="https://t.co/6Sv20SBqIr">pic.twitter.com/6Sv20SBqIr</a></p>— ESPN (@espn) <a href="https://x.com/espn/status/2104727970367557899?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Maldonado, originario de Brighton Park, también es el mánager y productor del grupo. Dijo que el mariachi ha interpretado el himno nacional para los White Sox, Cubs, Bulls, Blackhawks y los Detroit Tigers.</p><p>Desde el lunes, Maldonado dijo que ha recibido mensajes de apoyo de personas que viven desde Canadá hasta México.</p><p>“Esta presentación es extremadamente especial... especialmente si eres mexicano o mexicoamericano y vives en este país”, dijo Maldonado, de 42 años. “Me veo reflejado en esta presentación, y creo que por eso la gente está reaccionando”.</p><p>Maldonado inició el grupo en 2016 para ampliar el alcance de la música de mariachi y llevarla a una nueva generación.</p><p>“La música de mariachi ya no está en la radio como antes”, dijo. “Juan Gabriel, Chente y todos los grandes ya no suenan en la radio, así que hay una nueva generación de niños creciendo sin esa música. Estos son grandes momentos de proyección para la música de mariachi”.</p><p>La presentación del grupo en el juego de los Bears sí provocó una reacción de conservadores en internet, con algunos usuarios en X —como el grupo republicano Chicago Young Republicans— acusando a la NFL de ser “woke” o progresista. Maldonado dijo que no se detiene en los comentarios negativos y que, en cambio, se enfoca en cómo la presentación unió a las audiencias.</p><p>“Eso no tiene nada que ver con nosotros”, dijo sobre las distintas reacciones. “Tenemos muchos amigos en el mundo de las celebridades que nos escribieron. Incluso algunos jugadores de los Bears se comunicaron. La parte emocionante [fue] cuando Caleb Williams lo volvió a compartir con sus seguidores. Fue increíble. Es simplemente un momento que está uniendo a todos, y eso lo hace aún más emocionante”.</p><p>El grupo combina con éxito otras formas de música latina en sus presentaciones, que los han llevado por toda Norteamérica. La Ciudad de México es actualmente su principal mercado para el streaming de su música, dijo.</p><p>“Cuando escuchan la música, entienden que esto es algo completamente diferente. Es algo totalmente espectacular, y eso es la música de mariachi: un gigante dormido en la música latina”, dijo Maldonado. “Estamos muy orgullosos de ofrecer nuestra música al mundo”.</p><div honor llevar la música de mariachi al mundo.</p><p>“Fue sumamente emocionante y una gran fuente de orgullo. Al final, el deporte y la música son cosas que unen al mundo entero y a todas las culturas. Así que, para nosotros, Mariachi Herencia de México, interpretar el himno en Estados Unidos fue realmente un honor”, dijo Dueñas.</p><p>Maldonado dijo que sabe que la mayoría en el estadio no se dio cuenta de que el grupo es de Chicago.</p><p>“Apuesto que la mitad o la mayoría de ese estadio ni siquiera se dio cuenta de que este es el mariachi de su ciudad”, dijo Maldonado. “Nuestro estudio está ubicado en la Old Record Row, en la Michigan Avenue, donde antes se hacían el blues y la gran música de Chess Records. Ahí grabamos nuestra música, y simplemente estamos orgullosos de ser de aquí”.</p><p>El grupo planea grabar pronto un nuevo álbum en honor a las canciones del gran Juan Gabriel, ya fallecido. También planea un show navideño con música de la película “Home Alone”, que fue filmada en Chicago.</p><p><i>Michael Puente es reportero y presentador de WBEZ. entries.title: Bears report: RB D'Andre Swift misses practice with knee injury
entries.summary: <p>What happened Thursday at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Halas Hall</a>:</p><h3>No Swift</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/01/bears-jets-predictions-picks-week-4-odds-point-spread-new-york-chicago-soldier-field-nfl" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back D'Andre Swift did not practice Thursday because of a knee injury. He was not on the team's injury report for their walk-through a day earlier and ran 20 times for 84 yards against the Eagles on Monday night. If the knee continues to be a problem, the Bears would lean on Kyle Monangai, who had 10 carries for 31 yards last year. Friday's injury report will be telling for Swift, who missed only one game last season.</p><h3>Kyler still at it</h3><p>Slot cornerback Kyler Gordon practiced for the first time since the spring after the Bears' opened his 21-day window to return before Wednesday's walk-through. Gordon has battled a calf injury since offseason workouts, much to the frustration of his bosses, and has trained both inside and outside Halas Hall.</p><p>"I've got extreme confidence in what he can do when he's out there on the field —  and so that's never wavered," defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. "I think as we all know, the biggest thing for Kyler is for him to be healthy and be able to stay healthy. And so that's kind of where the focus is. You know, obviously when we get to a point where he's been able to get himself into football shape, be able to stay healthy, I see him being back out on the field for us and helping us win a lot of games."</p><h3>Caleb still out</h3><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams didn't practice, continuing his streak of sitting out since he pulled his hamstring against the Vikings. </p><p>Left tackle Braxton Jones, whom head coach Ben Johnson calls "week-to-week," didn't practice.</p><p>Defensive tackle Grady Jarrett and Joe Thuney got veteran days off Thursday, while Cam Lewis (hip) was limited. Guard Jonah Jackson, who was on Wednesday's injury report for personal reasons, was a full participant.<br></p>

entries.title: Dolton man killed during Oakbrook Center mall shooting; injured woman still hospitalized
entries.summary: <p>A Dolton man was killed, and four people are in custody Thursday, including a woman who was hospitalized after the shooting at Oakbrook Center mall, according to Oak Brook police.</p><p>Justin Hill, 28, and of Dolton, was dead on the scene of the Wednesday morning attack, according to police, who said two males and one female, remain in custody at the Oak Brook police station while a woman who was hospitalized was also in custody, police said. </p><p>Her condition, at a local medical facility, was not disclosed but police said an officer has been assigned to assist with security there as the investigation progresses. </p><p>Earlier, at a Wednesday afternoon news conference, Oak Brook police chief Brian Strockis said that around noon, two vehicles pulled into the parking lot outside the mall's LL Bean store, where an altercation occurred before occupants inside fired several shots.</p><p>Police were able to find another vehicle involved in the shooting by using <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" >license plate reader cameras</a> in Oak Brook. Occupants of that car were taken into custody for questioning in neighboring Oakbrook Terrace.</p><p>Strockis said it was still unclear what motivated the meetup or the shooting, though the department expects to release more information about the investigation. </p><p>In an earlier statement posted on social media, Oak Brook police said the mall remained open despite the earlier heavy police presence, as several agencies responded to the scene.</p><p>"Oakbrook Center is and will remain the premier shopping destination in the Midwest, and the safety of everyone who lives, works, and visits here remains our highest priority," Strockis said.</p>

entries.title: How Blackhawks' Roman Kantserov, Anton Frondell help each other learn English hockey terms
entries.summary: <p>SALT LAKE CITY — The rate at which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> rookie Roman Kantserov has learned English over the past couple years has amazed everyone.</p><p>By <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/29/blackhawks-roman-kantserov-nhl-preparation-english-spencer-knight" >chatting</a> with two Americans on his Russian team, watching American movies and simply dedicating himself to it, the 22-year-old native of Magnitogorsk — an industrial city near the Russia/Kazakhstan border — has picked up the language remarkably quickly. He's fully conversational at this point.</p><p>But the past few weeks, as the Hawks raced through an intense training camp and then hit the road for their opening trip, represented the final boss of English for Kantserov.</p><p>It's one thing to order coffee or joke around with teammates. It's another to decipher coach Jeff Blashill's specific drill instructions in a loud, chaotic rink environment when there are consequences for messing up. "Hockey English" can be its own language.</p><p>"Sometimes it's so hard because you don't know these things," Kantserov said Wednesday. "Every day, you learn and learn. You just listen and hear so many times one word, and you analyze, 'What does this mean?' </p><p>"Now I know 'hook and ladder' and 'rims' and 'regroups.' It's good. We help each other. Guys will help me. I ask [Nick Lardis] what we do because it was so fast. He says, 'Similar exercise.'"</p><p>Swedish rookie Anton Frondell found himself in the same situation when joining the Hawks last spring. Although his English was also remarkably good, he still encountered an overwhelming amount of newness. </p><p>When the Hawks flew to Seattle in April, for example, he wasn't sure where they were. Once they made it to San Jose — which he had heard of — he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/06/blackhawks-anton-frondell-observing-nhl-connor-bedard-power-play-sacha-boisvert" >realized</a> they must be on the West Coast. Now, he uses his Snapchat map to discover the locations of cities like Winnipeg (where his good friend Viggo Bjorck now plays).</p><p>He also had to memorize the team's daily routine on the fly. What time does the bus for morning skate leave? What time does the team go on the ice for warmups? Navigating those logistics becomes second nature for veteran NHL players, but it wasn't simple for Frondell at first.</p><p>Understanding the barrage of English hockey terms posed another challenge. And even though Frondell's month of experience last spring helped him build a foundation, he and Kantserov have been sharing notes this fall.</p><p>"For me, it's easy to talk to him because we are on the same level — kind of — with English," Frondell said. "I still don't understand everything that every guy says in here, so we're probably on the same page."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-credit"><p>John Locher/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>They're humble about it, but they've awed everyone with their ability and eagerness to learn. </p><p>Patrick Kane has brought up Kantserov's communication skills several times. Ryan Donato, asked last week which youngster had stood out most, singled out Frondell and his trustworthy "veteran-type presence." Coach Jeff Blashill has been impressed, too.</p><p>"We try to be consistent in our verbiage," Blashill said. "If they don’t understand something in our verbiage, they ask. They’re both really dialed-in young guys. They’re not afraid to ask questions, and they seem to learn quickly."</p><p>It works to Kantserov and Frondell's advantage, of course, that they're naturally outgoing, talkative people, regardless of language.</p><p>They're eager to socialize, even with reporters. Kantserov, coming off his "emotional" NHL debut Tuesday, apologized Wednesday for his occasionally redundant answers.</p><p>"I need to improve my [grammar], and I need to learn some other words," he said. "Because I think in every interview, I'm asked similar questions and I answer in the same words."</p><p>He added that he should "watch more movies," referencing the fact that much of his original English knowledge came from watching Transformers and Spider-Man.</p><h3><b>What about Levshunov?</b></h3><p>It can be tiring to talk in your non-native language all day, every day, so it's nice for Kantserov to have Belarusian defenseman Artyom Levshunov on the team. When they talk to each other, it is in Russian.</p><p>But Kantserov jokingly chided Levshunov for not being particularly helpful when it comes to understanding what's happening in practice.</p><p>"Arty is here, but sometimes he's so quiet," Kantserov said, grinning. "Maybe I ask him something and he won't tell me what to do. I ask him what to do in a drill, and he's like, 'You can see it. It's not hard. It's easy. You can see it by yourself.' I say, 'OK, brother. I figure out. Don't worry.'"</p><h3><b>Reminiscent of Panarin?</b></h3><p>The on-ice chemistry between Kane and Kantserov — although they're now split apart in the line combinations — has reminded some fans of Kane's natural connection with former Hawks star Artemi Panarin.</p><p>Kane doesn't really see it, though. For one thing, Panarin is right-handed and Kantserov is left-handed. Their playing styles differ, too.</p><p>"[Panarin was] very puck-dominant, puck-controlling, able to control the game with the way he carried the puck," Kane said. "Roman's got that ability, but he's more of an off-the-puck guy. He can find open spaces and find ways to get his shot off."</p>

entries.title: Despite clown show at the top, local FBI still ‘very good at what they do’
entries.summary: <p>When the FBI called, I hesitated.</p><p>Their request was simple enough. They wanted to bring me into headquarters, for briefings, once a week, for a couple months. Something called the FBI Citizens Academy.</p><p>Why me? Agents in the Chicago office were readers. Flattering, though, the way my mind works, I instantly saw that this wasn't necessarily a compliment — it was entirely possible that my perspective was seen as so woefully ignorant of the world of law enforcement, they felt duty bound to help me get a clue.</p><p>Or maybe they just wanted to get me in their clutches. I'd end up handcuffed to a metal chair in a basement, a bright light shining in my face.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-160000" name="module-160000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>One evening a week, for a couple hours, at their Roosevelt Road field office, learning the ins and outs of the department, the problems they face. Battling international terrorism, tracking cybercriminals and bank robbers.</p><p>"It sounds like traffic school," I told my wife.</p><p>But I have a personal rule: if you don't go, you never find out. Plus they would feed us — dinner from a different restaurant each week. Being fed always helps. I signed up.</p><p>This was in 2010, so the specific program details do not pop out in mind. There were guest lecturers, short films, tours of their facility. I knew several of the attendees, and the academy was pretty much the entirety of my social life for a while.</p><p>What's strongest is the sense I took away about the Federal Bureau of Investigation. They were good people, working hard, battling bad guys. I'm sure that was the point. Not that the bureau's often checkered history was whitewashed. Anyone who read Jonathan Eig's recent Pulitzer Prize winning biography of Martin Luther King knows how the FBI bugged King's hotel rooms, using the transcripts to try to blackmail him into silence, to urge him to kill himself, generating dirt they fed to his enemies. Knows that the FBI often strayed from protecting America to protecting a narrow right wing racist image of America.</p><p>But they were upfront about their past, if I recall correctly, and seemingly committed to a future of fighting crime rather than committing it. Plus they gave us all sorts of cool FBI swag — folders and baseball caps and T-shirts and gym bags and neat little commemorative medallions. Swag helps.</p><p>I felt invested; I still use the gym bag. So even though the past 20 months of Trump 2.0 have been a holy war against the federal government — from Elon Musk shredding departments and seizing data, to wrecking the National Park Service, to USAID being cut by 90%, leading to uncounted deaths around the world, to the Department of Education being cut 40%, and on and on, the entire federal government slashed by 10%, with the money saved handed back to rich people —somehow I found myself thinking about the local FBI office.</p><p>Maybe because of the spectacularly inept FBI director, Kash Patel, who would be considered a grotesque, improbable, perhaps racist caricature in a Christopher Buckley novel, but is all too real. From misuse of FBI jets to tales of excessive drinking, Patel has set a gold standard for clownishness and incompetency that stands out even against fierce competition from such future Toxic Bumbler Hall of Famers as health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. and secretary of war Pete Hegseth.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e40000" name="image-e40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/59646d4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5159x2895+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F3c%2Fbf0517dc4d07818bad3f549b521d%2Fimmigration-judge-arrested.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/11f18ce/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5159x2895+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F3c%2Fbf0517dc4d07818bad3f549b521d%2Fimmigration-judge-arrested.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d81b053/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5159x2895+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F3c%2Fbf0517dc4d07818bad3f549b521d%2Fimmigration-judge-arrested.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="FBI Director Kash Patel. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d81b053/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5159x2895+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F3c%2Fbf0517dc4d07818bad3f549b521d%2Fimmigration-judge-arrested.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0bfa038/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5159x2895+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F3c%2Fbf0517dc4d07818bad3f549b521d%2Fimmigration-judge-arrested.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d81b053/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5159x2895+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F3c%2Fbf0517dc4d07818bad3f549b521d%2Fimmigration-judge-arrested.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>FBI Director Kash Patel. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Alex Brandon/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>We haven't even mentioned the direct damage to the department's reputation, from publicly announcing that a record of bestiality would no longer prevent someone from becoming an FBI agent to what is being called " the gravest intelligence breach of the FBI in history — and perhaps one of the worst in all of U.S. history," the hacking of the personnel files of current and past FBI agents.</p><p>This led me to worry about the morale of my pals at the Chicago office. Somehow, the direct approach — ask the office — seemed both time-consuming and fruitless. At best I'd get administration spin. So I deployed some stealthing of my own and called an experienced local law enforcement official who deals with the Chicago FBI on a regular basis.</p><p>"They're still very good at what they do," he said, asking that his name not be used due to the circumspection instinctive to law enforcement types. "Their traditions are very strong. They will weather this well."</p><p>Good to hear. Not that "this" is anywhere near over. Even we optimists can, at best, hold out hope that we are seeing, to quote Churchill, "not the end... not even the beginning of the end" but "perhaps, the end of the beginning."</p><p>Of course, Churchill said that in 1942. Still a long, difficult slog ahead with many battles to fight and win, and success in no way certain. </p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Stinging from playoff exit, Cubs must make sure next year is different: ‘It’s time to look in the mirror’
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?</p><p>It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/01/cubs-padres-playoffs-mlb-postseason-game-2-elimination-alex-bregman-pete-crow-armstrong-matthew-boyd" >Bowing out of the postseason after two games</a>, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?</p><p>They didn’t come close.</p><p>“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.</p><p>“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.</p><p>“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”</p><p>In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?</p><p>It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.</p><p>Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.</p><p>“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’</p><p>“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”</p><p>With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.</p><p>But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.</p><p>What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?</p><p>That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.</p><p>This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.</p><p>The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.</p><p>“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”</p><p>Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.</p><p>Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.</p><p>Then there’s the corner outfielders.</p><p>Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.</p><p>Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.</p><p>“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.</p><p>Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.</p><p>“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”</p><p>With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:</p><p>How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Policía de Chicago acusado de golpear a una adolescente durante confrontación captada en un video viral
entries.summary: <p>Un sargento de la Policía de Chicago, envuelto en una controversia, fue acusado de golpear a una joven de 17 años mientras ella grababa un video que luego se volvió viral y en el que se veía al agente amenazando a un grupo de niños este verano en el lado suroeste.</p><p>Jeremy Sikorski, de 45 años y residente de Garfield Ridge, enfrenta cargos graves de agresión agravada por el presunto ataque del 9 de agosto en la cuadra 5100 al sur de Merrimac Avenue, según registros judiciales del Condado de Cook. Sikorski se entregó a la policía la semana pasada.</p><p>Sikorski y su familia asistían a una parrillada cuando él y otros dos hombres se acercaron a un grupo de adolescentes en un callejón, dijeron los fiscales en una presentación ante la corte. Los fiscales indicaron que el video muestra a Sikorski regañando a uno de los muchachos por estar “molestando” a otros niños, al parecer en referencia a una pelea anterior en un parque que involucró a por lo menos uno de los hijos de Sikorski.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e90000" name="module-e90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Luego, Sikorski se acercó a una adolescente y primero la amenazó con darle una bofetada; después le advirtió que le iba a “dar en la m----” mientras levantaba el puño, dijeron los fiscales, según el video. Sikorski también habría amenazado con golpear a los padres de la menor y amedrentó a otra persona.</p><p>Después de que Sikorski empezó a alejarse, se dio la vuelta y golpeó en la cabeza a la joven de 17 años, dijeron los fiscales. El teléfono de ella cayó al suelo y se le escuchó “llorando de dolor”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">We have been informed that the man in this video is a Chicago police sergeant. <br><br>The name we have been given matches a known CPD sergeant, but we have not confirmed the identity, so we're withholding that info for now.<br><br>Details coming... <a href="https://t.co/tSkUgS1Svr">pic.twitter.com/tSkUgS1Svr</a></p>— CWBChicago (@CWBChicago) <a href="https://x.com/CWBChicago/status/2086920780172960196?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Días después, le diagnosticaron una conmoción cerebral, dijeron las autoridades. Los fiscales señalaron que ella y otras cinco personas identificaron a Sikorski como el agresor en una rueda de reconocimiento fotográfica.</p><p>El video del incidente fue publicado por CWB Chicago, un blog enfocado en temas de crimen y seguridad pública.</p><p>Sikorski no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios de su abogado. Un abogado de la familia de la joven se negó a comentar.</p><p>El presunto ataque, al parecer, fue provocado por una discusión anterior entre los adolescentes a los que Sikorski confrontó y un grupo de adolescentes más jóvenes, descritos por los fiscales como los hijos de Sikorski y del anfitrión de la parrillada.</p><p>Uno de los jóvenes mayores terminó dándole una patada en el estómago a uno de los menores, dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>Más tarde, Sikorski confrontó a los adolescentes mayores en el callejón de su casa y les preguntó si estaban acosando a los niños más pequeños, lo que desembocó en el ataque, dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>Cuando la policía respondió a una llamada por una agresión, la madre de uno de los niños mayores les dijo que los menores habían sido quienes iniciaron el conflicto, dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>A Sikorski le retiraron sus facultades policiales dos días después, informó la policía. La Oficina Civil de Responsabilidad Policial (COPA) abrió una investigación administrativa sobre el incidente.</p><p>Sikorski se entregó el 22 de septiembre en el Distrito Central para enfrentar los cargos, según su informe de arresto. La petición de los fiscales para que permaneciera detenido en la Cárcel del Condado de Cook fue rechazada durante su primera audiencia judicial el 23 de septiembre.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Rosemary Sobol </i><br><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Englewood lawn care workers targeted in 20-minute armed robbery spree
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a man who robbed three separate lawn care workers at gunpoint in a 20-minute span in Englewood Monday morning. </p><p>In all attacks, the man demanded the workers' cell phones and wallets, most recently at 9:50 a.m. in the 5500 block of South Ashland Avenue, police said. </p><p>The robber, wearing all black including a mask, then sped away in a car to the 5500 block of South Union Avenue where he robbed someone else at 9:47 a.m. The first heist occurred about 9:30 a.m. in the 5900 block of South Parnell Avenue, police said. </p><p>No injuries were reported. </p><p>Anyone with information should contact Area 1 detectives at 312-747-8380. </p>

entries.title: Why losing industrial jobs hit differently in Detroit, Milwaukee and Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Chris Gerben grew up in the metro Detroit area in the 1980s and ’90s, and even as a child, he noticed a lot of major shifts in the city.</p><p>“We were a steel mill town, and in the mid ’80s is when a lot of this kind of emptying-out of the city was happening,” Gerben said.</p><p>He remembers going to at least three different elementary schools because teachers kept getting laid off.</p><p>From the peak of Detroit’s auto industry until Gerben was born, roughly three decades, the city lost over 200,000 jobs — more than during the Great Depression. It also lost more than half a million people.</p><p>Gerben now lives with his family in Chicago, and he wonders if what happened in Detroit happened across the Midwest in the same way. How did deindustrialization hit Milwaukee? And why was Chicago seemingly spared?</p><p>“If you don't know any better … it would seem like, ‘Oh, [Chicago] is privileged in some way,’” Gerben said.</p><p>Deindustrialization shaped the Midwest in ways seen and unseen. We look back at how things differed across cities when it came to the industries that built them up and how each city dealt with the fall out of losing so much.</p><h3><b>The Motor City</b></h3><p>More than a century ago, the “Big Three” automakers — General Motors, Ford and Chrysler — made a home in Detroit, which led to more cars being built in the Motor City than anywhere in the world.</p><p>These factory jobs attracted the first wave of the Great Migration — African Americans leaving the rural South for the urban North, starting in the 1910s — as well as immigrant workers. Marsha Battle-Fillpot said her dad, Joe Von Battle, was one of those early workers coming up from Georgia.</p><p>“The auto industry here allowed for a relative prosperity that was unprecedented,” Battle-Fillpot says. “It’s sort of not viewed like that, with all the bells and whistles of, say, a New York, but this place is no joke.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A portrait of Marsha Battle-Fillpot.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jimmy Gutierrez/WUWM</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Von Battle was laid off from the auto plant when white workers returned to the factory after World War II. This gave rise to the axiom “last hired, first fired” with regard to Black workers.</p><p>“He was so despondent about [facing] a reversal like that, he vowed at that point he would never work for another man,” Battle-Fillpot said.</p><p>With the prosperity of the auto industry lifting all boats, Von Battle decided to start his own business. In 1945, he opened Joe’s Record Shop in the city’s historic Black Bottom neighborhood. It was an instant hit: In the first two years, he had over $100,000 worth of records in stock.</p><p>But in the ’50s, the Big Three started pulling out of the city, moving to the suburbs for cheaper land.</p><p>This began well before the “<a class="Link" href="https://beltmag.com/detroit-67-rebellion-matters-now/" target="_blank" ><u>Rebellion of ’67</u></a>,” five days of racial unrest in late July 1967 during which 43 people died, hundreds reported injuries and police arrested more than 7,000 people.</p><p>“There’s a whole narrative that says that, well, Detroit was basically doing okay until 1967 and all the whites left, and then Detroit fell into decline,” Battle-Fillpot said. “That’s just so wrong-headed. There’s no statistics that bear that out.”</p><p>In over 20 years since opening, Joe’s Record Shop became a symbol of Black art and opportunity that defined the time. During the Rebellion, it was looted.</p><p>“When my father walked back into that store … and he saw the destruction, I really say that my dad really died then,” Battle-Fillpot said. “He tried to reopen after that, even, but he was just unable to gather it back altogether.”</p><p>Today, headquarters for the Big Three automakers are still in metro Detroit, but jobs in the city never bounced back.</p><h3><b>‘The Machine Shop of the World’</b></h3><p>The story of industry and its demise echoed in Milwaukee, the home of beer and brewing, heavy manufacturing, and iron and steel, also called ‘The Machine Shop of the World’. There, industry here was more diverse than Detroit, which went all-in on the auto industry. With a bustling port and growing rail system, Milwaukee was critical to the economy of the Wisconsin region.</p><p>“‘Blue-collar’ in Milwaukee meant middle class,” says Adam Carr, a public historian and artist in the city. “That’s entwined with the history of socialism here, that the worker was not a chump in Milwaukee.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-credit"><p>Jimmy Gutierrez/WUWM</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>An image that, for Carr, exemplifies the city’s indigenous roots, its peak in industry and the decline is Three Bridges Park — an old brownfield turned into a sprawling park, filled with walking paths built over a freeway that cut through the city.</p><p>The loss of jobs and wealth in Milwaukee, specifically <a class="Link" href="https://www.milwaukeeindependent.com/featured/reggie-jackson-impact-deindustrialization-milwaukees-inner-city/" target="_blank" ><u>Black and Latino Milwaukee</u></a>, went down just like in Detroit. Urban renewal brought in freeways but also displaced families in lower income neighborhoods. Redlining discriminatorily shut people out of certain neighborhoods. This stunted generational wealth, a history the city is still dealing with. Like Detroit, industry jobs never bounced back.</p><p>“I heard someone say, ‘Pie in the sky in Milwaukee was the factory job,’” Carr remembers. “We thought the gravy train would never end. And I think we haven’t found exactly who we are after industry yet.”</p><h3><b>The Second City</b></h3><p>In Chicago’s West Loop neighborhood, built on a graveyard of old industry, you’ll find the University of Illinois Chicago’s Cuppa Hall and the Great Cities Institute.</p><p>Associate director Matt Wilson studies the long shadow of deindustrialization in Chicago. He says historically, the city had a lot of the same advantages as Milwaukee and Detroit: natural resources, a bustling port. What separated Chicago was the rail system — and as the country pushed west, Chicago became a major hub.</p><p>“Chicago still has that identity of the crossroads. A lot of goods flow through here,” Wilson says. “It’s really easy, when you go on the river, to see barge traffic, and when you go to any of the ports that are around the city, you see the large-scale movement of goods.”</p><p>Industry varied in Chicago. The famous Union Stock Yards was considered the meatpacking center of the world. Then, in the 1980s, the city pivoted.</p><p>“Chicago needs to compete with other cities to attract jobs in corporate headquarters,” Wilson says. “It needs to bring in tourism and make sure all the hotels are filled and that there's a nightlife.”</p><p>Tax incentives and tax dollars were funneled to rebuild Downtown, though not other parts of the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" The historic factory was transformed into the centerpiece of the Pullman National Historical Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“The neighborhood of South Chicago, on the southeast side of the city, it feels like [it’s] from the historical archives I’ve read, that the center of gravity was the steel plant,” Wilson says.</p><p>Until the early 2000s, that included Pressed Steel, Republic Steel, Wisconsin Steel and the big one, U.S. Steel. These plants were the source of middle-class employment, which stabilized the housing market and both retail and commercial businesses.</p><p>“Both my grandfathers worked [in the plants]. My dad worked there and I worked there,” says Michael Lisecki, who grew up in South Chicago. “It was like everybody worked in one of the mills, whether it was U.S., Wisconsin. It was devastating when we all got laid off.”</p><p>Lisecki started working in the mills in 1978 when he was 18, making better money than he ever dreamed possible. Three years later, he was laid off and the neighborhood was never the same.</p><p>Chicago pivoted to a post-industry chapter earlier than Detroit and Milwaukee. But no matter the city, deindustrialization left a hole, and it’s clear the bones of the past are still with us.</p><p><i>Curious Midwest is a limited series collaboration with Curious City, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.wuwm.com/bubblertalk" target="_blank" ><i><u>Bubbler Talk at WUWM</u></i></a><i> in Milwaukee and </i><a class="Link" href="https://wdet.org/podcasts/curiosid-podcast/" target="_blank" ><i><u>CuriosiD at WDET</u></i></a><i> in Detroit. entries.title: Bulls and Caleb Wilson getting defensive in first week of training camp
entries.summary: <p>Tiago Splitter wasn’t being coy as much as he was actually showing his hand.</p><p>The topic was defense — a topic the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> coach holds close to his heart — and specifically who would be the best option to guard opposing starting power forwards this season?</p><p>After all, that was a role that Patrick Williams was supposed to still be holding down since he was drafted in 2020 but has instead turned into a by-committee over that span. From Alex Caruso to Isaac Okoro to Matas Buzelis, Bulls coaches have tried them all.</p><p>Now, it just might fall in the hands of the rook.</p><p>Reminder: Caleb Wilson not only welcomes that but welcomes it with his usual bravado.</p><p>“I’m going to go do what’s gotta be done,” Wilson said of guarding the elite power forwards in the Association. “That’s the type of dude I am. Of course, it doesn’t really matter who I’m playing against because they gotta guard me too.</p><p>“I’m going to go out there and be as physical as I can. Of course I’ve gotta learn some tough stages but I’m comfortable guarding whoever they put in front of me.”</p><p>And that’s where it could get very interesting for the Bulls and Splitter.</p><p>Yes, with a projected starting five of Josh Giddey, Norman Powell, Buzelis, Wilson and Nic Claxton it could be Wilson that gets the first crack, which means Buzelis can move to a more natural three spot for him, but it also means Splitter knows this group is versatile enough defensively to matchup a lot of different ways.</p><p>Take opposing point guards for example.</p><p>Splitter sounded very comfortable deploying a variety of different looks at the other team on any given night.</p><p>Asked who would guard the point guard right after declaring Wilson would probably be locked on a four, Splitter replied, “Who is the point guard? Like who are we playing against? Some nights Caleb might guard him, some nights Josh, some Norman, some Matas. It depends. We might put Nic on a point guard. We gotta see what is the matchup, who are we playing against, and we’ll figure it out.”</p><p>That’s why Wilson is not only getting training camp minutes in the paint defensively but going through a boot camp of learning perimeter defense.</p><p>“I think with Caleb, one of the things we’ve been talking about is teaching him how to guard on the perimeter,” Splitter said. “He’s been guarding his whole life, especially in college, he’s been guarding mostly as a four, a five, as a big, so now he has to get used to being on the perimeter and navigate screens, going over, under … those little things he’s got to learn and it’s part of the development. We want to be more aggressive (on defense).”</p><p>He might have a group to do that, especially from a length standpoint.</p><p>Claxton is listed at 6-foot-11, Wilson is up to 6-10, Buzelis 6-8, Giddey 6-8 and Powell a mere 6-4. Even the bench has 6-10 Leonard Miller, 6-8 Jalen Smith, and 6-9 Zach Collins.</p><p>“Clax, Caleb, having Lenny, we’re a really tall team,” Buzelis said of the defense. “I remember walking in (the other day), and I was just looking around like, ‘Man, we’re pretty big.’ We’ve got a lot of fours, guys that can make plays, athleticism. That just makes you more comfortable defensively.”</p><p>A nice comfort to have. Then again, not that Wilson really needs it.</p><p>“Every matchup is different,” Wilson added of his role defensively. “You’ll have your advantages and disadvantages, but over time, the stronger I get, I feel like I have an advantage in every way.”</p>

entries.title: NIPSCO apologizes as Gary residents take their anger to the statehouse
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was originally published in </i><a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/nipsco-statehouse-committee-hearing/" target="_blank" ><i>Capital B Gary</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>The president of NIPSCO apologized to the people of Gary and others on Tuesday for not including their cities in a plan that it published to restore power days after the Aug. 11 storm.</p><p>The company did not intend to deprioritize those cities, which included Portage, Lake Station, and Griffith, but did not include them because it was still assessing their damage and was unable to offer an estimated time of restoration then, said Vince Parisi, the company’s president and chief operating officer.</p><p>“We did not want to provide an estimate that we could not substantiate. But we should have communicated that more effectively to our customers at that time and I’m sorry for any confusion that caused,” Parisi said.</p><p>Parisi offered the apology while speaking at the Indiana Statehouse on Tuesday as part of lawmakers’ first public look into the storm.</p><p>The hearing revealed new insights about why Gary went without power for two to three weeks after the storm. It also presented NIPSCO’s plan for figuring out what went wrong and what they might have been able to do better. And it offered insight into some of the changes that lawmakers are considering instituting to ensure more efficient responses to future power outages.</p><p>Tempers flared at times as participants grappled with the physical and psychological toll of the storm, which left thousands of Gary residents without electricity for a prolonged period. More than 7 weeks afterward, feelings were still raw about what happened. On more than one occasion, the chair of the committee reminded speakers to keep their tone and comments respectful as they gave testimony.</p><p>Ten members of the public were allowed to speak, including five from Gary. Carolyn McCrady of Gary made the bus ride down to Indianapolis with roughly 20 other Gary and Northwest Indiana residents, and she spoke candidly during her allotted time on the House floor.</p><p>“I can tell you that people in Gary are angry,” McCrady told the audience. “Angry because our bills are too high and scared also that the next storm will cause as much or even more destruction. We are particularly worried about the coming winter months, when a blackout like the one we just experienced would threaten the very lives of many people who do not have generators or other options to survive without heat.”</p><p>The hearing follows news last week that state regulators have begun <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/nipsco-gary-power-outages-investigation/" target="_blank" >an official investigation</a> into NIPSCO’s response to the storm. That one could last years. But Parisi said the utility’s internal investigation of the storm would be complete by Thanksgiving. NIPSCO also said it was hiring a third party to conduct an independent investigation.</p><p>Still, NIPSCO’s testimony Tuesday shed more light on what went wrong. Vegetation management “wasn’t the issue” during the storm, Parisi told the committee that held the meeting, the Interim Study Committee on Energy, Utilities and Telecommunications.</p><p>Parisi said utility poles failed because they were meant to withstand 55 mph winds, not the 100 mph gusts that came with the storm. NIPSCO said 1,500 utility poles were damaged during the storm, whereas in the five previous storms, the average number of damaged poles was 90.</p><p>Gary took the brunt of the damage, ending up with more outages than any other community in Northwest Indiana, Parisi said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Volunteers clear trees in front of a home on Van Buren Street near 20th Place in Gary, Ind., Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Asked by a senator how many poles fell because trees pulled down power lines versus how many were snapped by the wind, Parisi said he didn’t have that data and has yet to look at the age of the poles that failed.</p><p>A Gary resident who spoke during the public comment period contested Parisi’s narrative that overgrown trees did not contribute to power outages.</p><p>“I’ve been in my home for 15 years now, and NIPSCO has never come out [to trim trees],” Sherry Smith, 65, told Capital B Gary. “I have a huge NIPSCO pole and heavy trees in my yard.”</p><p>NIPSCO is also facing a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing the company of negligent vegetation management. The lawsuit, <a class="Link" href="https://dockets.justia.com/docket/indiana/inndce/2:2026cv00459/130025" target="_blank" >Tipold v. NIPSCO</a>, was moved last week at the utility’s request from Porter County to U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana in Hammond.</p><p>Ryan Baker, president of United Steelworkers Local 12775, which represents NIPSCO workers, testified that the utility’s staffing choices contributed to the prolonged power outage in Northwest Indiana. With 183 linemen, NIPSCO has fewer than at any time in the past 15 years, he said. The company has lost 50 linemen since 2020, he added.</p><p>“As we’ve seen staffing levels decrease, we’re finding it harder and harder to get our two resources matched up,” Baker explained. “So there may be line crews to restore the circuit, [but] there’s not a substation electrician available to restore the service, or vice versa. You may have the substation electrician available at one of the sites, but not a line crew to finish the assessing and repair work.”</p><p>During the recovery period immediately following the storm, NIPSCO contracted with electric crews from across the South and Midwest to repair the lines. Parisi told lawmakers NIPSCO relies on contract crews at times “for affordability reasons.” Baker said contractors usually cost more, and those costs get passed on to ratepayers.</p><p>Parisi’s apology was the second one the company gave to Gary about the list. The first apology came during a <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/gary-power-outage-nipsco-restoration-august-25/" target="_blank" >press conference</a> involving Melody Birmingham, executive vice president and utilities group president for NIPSCO parent company NiSource Inc.</p><p>Gary Mayor Eddie Melton, a former NIPSCO employee, asked lawmakers to require utilities statewide to provide restoration estimates for all communities.
