entries.title: New video shows Chicago police officers shooting armed man who later died
entries.summary: <p>Oversight officials released video footage Thursday that shows Chicago police officers shooting a man armed with a knife in the lobby of a River North hotel last year.</p><p>Prosecutors later said the shooting left Demond Williams with “limited brain activity” and that doctors didn't expect him to recover. Williams died July 26, but his cause and manner of death haven't been released, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>After the shooting, Williams was charged with felony counts of aggravated assault of a peace officer and illegal weapon possession that were dropped a month before he died, according to Cook County court records. A court order in the case had barred the Civilian Office of Police Accountability from releasing videos and reports related to the shooting.</p><p>The newly released video footage shows that officers first encountered Williams in the lobby of a building in the 100 block of West Hubbard Street on April 7, 2025. He then fled to a convenience store and was ultimately chased into the Courtyard by Marriott hotel at 30 E. Hubbard St., where he got into an elevator and a standoff ensued. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/LDu3XByUVxI?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="COPA releases video of police shooting man wielding a knife during standoff at River North hotel"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>When one officer fired a Taser at Williams, another cop noted that Williams' layers of clothing may have prevented the shock, the video shows. At least a dozen officers stood outside the elevator, with some calling Williams by his name and urging him to drop a knife and throw it outside of the elevator. </p><p>When Williams left the elevator, four officers deployed Tasers and two officers shot him, according to the records. Six shots rang out, and Williams turned back into the elevator and fell to the ground. </p><p>Officers handcuffed him and rendered aid after pulling him out of the elevator by his legs, video shows. Paramedics arrived six minutes after the shooting.</p><p>Williams was struck in his upper body and rushed to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in critical condition, along with two officers who were taken as a precaution. A knife was recovered at the scene, police said at the time.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/04/09/charges-filed-man-shot-by-police-river-north-courtyard-by-marriot" >Man shot by police in River North hotel faces assault, weapons charges</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/04/07/shooting-courtyard-marriott-shooting-downtown" >Man shot by police in River North hotel had a knife, police say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Daily Herald journalists clear vote to successfully form labor union
entries.summary: <p>Journalists of suburban publication the Daily Herald <a class="Link" href="https://newsguild.org/daily-herald-journalists-win-election-to-form-daily-herald-news-guild/" target="_blank" >officially voted</a> to form a labor union Thursday, according to the Daily Herald News Guild.</p><p>The 15-0 vote was observed by union and management officials at the National Labor Relations Board offices at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. The Daily Herald staff joined the Chicago News Guild Local 34071 TNG-CWA, which also represents journalists at the Sun-Times.</p><p>The union is now planning to poll its members to determine contract conditions and schedule bargaining sessions with management at Tribune Publishing.</p><p>Kevin Schmit, the Daily Herald’s associate sports editor and a 29-year employee, said the group was quickly united by the latest round of layoffs, and was fearful of what else could come due to it being the only non-union newsroom under the company.</p><p>“The Daily Herald was the outlier under the Tribune umbrella,” Schmit told the Sun-Times. “Every other one of their papers is unionized, so it was scary being the only one without that protection. You get the feeling anything they can’t do to the union shops, they were going to do to us.”</p><p>Tribune Publishing didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>In the last decade, the Daily Herald has been through eight rounds of buyouts and three rounds of layoffs, according to the union. Employees who survived the staff reductions saw at least a 15% pay cut and their workweek reduced to 36.5 hours.</p><p>The paper has covered suburban Chicago since 1872, and was independently owned and run by the Paddock family for four generations. In 2018, the Paddock family members sold portions of the company to its employees and set up an employee stock ownership plan.</p><p>Schmit said there had been rumblings of unionization under Paddock, but it never materialized.</p><p>The Daily Herald was acquired by Tribune Publishing in June after the company ran a full-page ad in the Chicago Tribune offering a higher price than Shaw Media, which owns other suburban papers and had previously been in talks to make a purchase.</p><p>That came after 12 of the paper’s staffers were laid off, including executive editor Lisa Miner, the paper’s copy desk and page designers.</p><p>“To be under this new place, and within a month or two lose 20% of our newsroom, it was just this body blow,” Schmit said. “But it was like jet fuel for our effort. That really upset all of us to the bone.”</p><p>All twenty union-eligible staffers signed cards in support of the union in August, though Tribune Publishing is currently contesting the eligibility of two staffers who they claim are supervisors, which reduced the vote count, Schmit said.</p><p>While it was frustrating that management refused to recognize the union voluntarily, he said the group “appreciated” the chance to show how they had come together.</p><p>"We could've saved a lot of time if they would have just voluntarily recognized us,” Schmit said. “If management or ownership had any thoughts about a lack of unity, we showed today we’re all together on this.”</p>

entries.title: Mayoral candidate John Kelly vows to use lobbyist clout to block Amtrak move to Bridgeport
entries.summary: <p>Mayoral challenger John Kelly on Thursday promised Bridgeport politicians and their constituents to use the clout he has built as White Sox lobbyist and Jerry Reinsdorf’s business partner to “stop Amtrak from coming into your neighborhood.”</p><p>Kelly made the promise while showcasing his political candor to an audience of movers and shakers at the City Club of Chicago.</p><p>Bridgeport Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) and Cook County Commissioner John Daley have been determined to prevent the Sox from leaving Rate Field for the South Loop <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >under a plan</a> proposed by Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia. That plan also entails the construction of the Amtrak maintenance site in Bridgeport.</p><p>Kelly is uniquely positioned to help. For nearly three decades, he has lobbied on behalf of clout-heavy clients that do business with City Hall and the state of Illinois. His state lobbying clients include the White Sox, whose principal owner Jerry Reinsdorf also is Kelly’s business partner in a security firm.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" >What to know about the Chicago White Sox stadium proposal</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>That’s why Kelly believes he is in a position to deliver for Bridgeport residents. </p><p>“Rahm Emanuel got elected because he was tough and he was competent. His line is, `As mayor, you make a decision every day. You have an `A’ and you have a `B.’ I had an A and a B down in Bridgeport when Amtrak wanted to jam a facility that would ruin their neighborhood,” Kelly told the City Club audience.</p><p>“I got in the car and I went down. Didn’t talk to any of my advisers. And we are gonna stop the Amtrak from coming to your neighborhood.”</p><p>After the smattering of applause died down, Kelly said, “Some candidates showed up. Some of them — their line was, `I can’t go down there because I’m on the fence on that issue.’ You can’t be mayor when you sit on the fence. That’s not gonna happen when I’m mayor of Chicago.”</p><p>Kelly predicted that the insider relationships he has built as a career lobbyist would be used against him in the crowded race for mayor.</p><p>“My opponents are gonna come at me and I’m sure they’ve got commercials in the can... [saying], `John’s a lobbyist.’ Sorry, lobbyists get s—t done,” Kelly said. “We’ve worked the system for 30 years and we know ins and outs better than anybody. And I don’t know why that is a negative, because I don’t believe that it is. “</p><p>Lee said she welcomes support from Kelly and anybody else who is prepared to help Bridgeport residents in the fight to stop Amtrak and keep the White Sox at Rate Field. But she has no idea whether Kelly has the clout to “pull that off."</p><p>She said Reinsdorf is in control of the team right now and that he was “unaware of what was happening with Amtrak.”</p><p>“I don’t know that the White Sox organization has any influence over Amtrak’s decisions, she said.</p><p>And even if Kelly’s clout could help, Lee said Bridgeport residents can’t wait for the outcome of the mayoral election.</p><p>“This is existential for us. Time is of the essence right now. The development team and Amtrak have told us they intend to get shovels in the ground as soon as the end of the year or [early] 2027,” Lee said.</p><p>The urgency of the matter has everything to do with what Lee called a “federal pre-exemption.” Amtrak received more than $600 million and a “categorical exclusion” from the federal government for the project, which allows it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>“They believe those powers allow them to bypass local zoning and building rules. They’re willing to coordinate and consult with the city. But by no means is it somehow asking for permission,” Lee said. “I’m trying to understand where federal pre-emption meets home rule authority because, at some point, they’re gonna need to tap a water line, tap a sewer line, close a street for construction. And I am unclear as to whether federal pre-emption gives them those rights.”</p><p></p><p>Arguing that billionaire businessman Ken Griffin was run out of Chicago because of violent crime, Kelly also vowed to “cut a deal with Griffin to get him back” and lure the $2 billion donation that Griffin gave to Carnegie Mellon University for a campus he's building in Florida.</p><p>And he warned the audience to "look out for Brandon Johnson," whom he claimed "won't be an easy lay-up of a candidate" because he's "got a conviction for what he believes in."</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Bears QB Tyson Bagent: 'Right decision' to report concussion symptoms even if it cost him an opportunity
entries.summary: <p>Longtime <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> backup quarterback Tyson Bagent made one of the most difficult decisions of his career last week when, knowing full well what it would cost, told the team about his concussion symptoms.</p><p>Bagent was over it by Monday when he watched third-stringer Case Keenum flourish against the Eagles in a start that would’ve been his, but the initial choice was grueling as his agent eventually convinced him protecting his health should come first.</p><p>“Your brain is far more important than being able to play in a game, no matter how high-stakes the game is,” Bagent said after practice Thursday. “We made the right decision.”</p><p>He was as supportive of Keenum as could be, saying, “I would like everything that the football world can offer me, but ... I have absolutely zero ego in this and nobody is a bigger cheerleader and fan of Case Keenum than I am. He’s the epitome of what I believe a quarterback is supposed to be.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9CeQSRrGu50?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Bears QB Tyson Bagent on watching teammate Case Keenum on Monday"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Keenum talked Thursday, too, and couldn’t say enough about how highly he thinks of Bagent, but ultimately the Bears’ starter against the Jets on Sunday will be picked by coach Ben Johnson’s criteria. Johnson has been tightlipped about Bagent, Keenum and injured starter Caleb Williams, although Williams was out of practice again Thursday and is almost certainly going to miss his second consecutive start.</p><p>Williams is recovering from a Grade 2 hamstring strain, which is a serious enough injury to keep a player out for a month or more.</p><p>That could factor into Johnson’s calculations. The decision is not necessarily whether he believes Keenum can give him one more great game, but rather if he thinks Bagent gives the Bears the best chance over the next few: home against the Jets, then at the Packers and Falcons.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/28/bears-inactives-vs-eagles-k-cairo-santos-cb-tyrique-stevenson-good-to-go" >Keenum was excellent in the 27-7 win over the Eagles</a> and completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and two touchdown passes for a 110.8 passer rating. He bristled when asked Thursday how he felt about the case he made to keep starting.</p><p>“I’ve been making my case for 15 years,” he said. “I’m trying to win ballgames. I didn’t go out there to try to make a case to be anybody except myself and I’m feeling pretty good about winning the football game.”</p><p>That’s great, and it was a memorable night. He has rarely in his career, however, sustained that level of play for a sustained stretch.</p><p>As Johnson looks at the long view, the quarterbacks are at vastly different stages. While Keenum is hanging on as tightly as he can at 38, Bagent is a 26-year-old upstart in whom the team sees enormous upside.</p><p>From the time he made the roster as an undrafted rookie from Division II Shepherd University in 2023, the Bears have believed Bagent was tracking toward a starting job. There was no chance it’d be with them, of course, once they drafted Williams, but the point is that he’s still on his way up.</p><p>Johnson has dodged the question multiple times in the past week, but has pointed out twice that Bagent beat out Keenum for the No. 2 quarterback job “for a reason.”</p><p>As was true for Keenum before Monday, Bagent hasn’t started a game since 2023.</p><p>Bagent navigated his five games (four starts) in place of Fields reasonably well given the circumstances. He was just months into his NFL career, and it’s a leap from facing Kutztown University to staring down Khalil Mack on “Sunday Night Football” in Los Angeles.</p><p>This opportunity is much more like taking the wheel of a Lamborghini, and Bagent is far more developed.</p><p>“It’s all on the mental side,” he said of his growth. “Now, being in a couple different systems and being in Ben’s system, I feel comfortable to execute, recognize coverages and play a lot faster.”</p><p>Johnson reminded a national audience Monday that his play designs and calls are as much the star of the show as any quarterback. Receivers were open all night, making decisions clear-cut for Keenum in the pocket.</p><p>There’s no doubt he thinks the offense will look just as good, maybe even better, with Bagent.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Johnson strikes $260.8M global settlement to resolve police misconduct cases involving ex-CPD Det. Guevara
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is proposing a $260.8 million global settlement to resolve en masse 16 police miscounduct lawsuits and compensate 17 plaintiffs framed for murders by corrupt former Chicago police Det. Reynaldo Guevara.</p><p>Forty-three people, including three women, have been exonerated after they were sent to prison on murder convictions in cases handled by Guevara in the 1980s and 1990s. Most of them lived in Humboldt Park.</p><p>As of last winter, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/02/07/wrongful-convictions-burge-guevara-watts-chicago" target="_blank" >lawsuits targeting him</a> had already cost the city and Cook County at least $80 million. In February, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/02/09/det-reynaldo-guevara-settlements-chicago-police-department-misconduct" target="_blank" >City Council approved another $29.2 million</a> in settlements linked to accusations of his police misconduct. A few weeks ago, $14 million more was added to the pile.</p><p>The $260.8 million global settlement on the agenda for Monday’s meeting of the City Council’s Finance Committee dwarf those earlier one-off settlements.</p><p>And it’s roughly three times higher than the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/02/victims-90-million-dollars-police-misconduct-settlement-chicago-police-ronald-watts" >$90 million global settlement </a>that put to rest 176 lawsuits tied to former Chicago Police Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was accused of framing hundreds of people on drug charges at the Chicago Housing Authority’s Ida B. Wells complex.</p><p>Ever since the Watts cases were resolved in package deal, the City Council has been pressured the Johnson administration to strike a similar global settlement, resolving dozens of remaining Guevara cases.</p><p>Retiring Corporation Counsel Mary Richardson-Lowry delivered that global settlement on her way out the door. She briefed Council members Thursday in what Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) called Richardson-Lowry’s “swan song.”</p><p>“We have a lot of these cases. Any time we can put them all together and package them and get a better settlement amount, it’s best for the taxpayers,” Dowell told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“If we had to defend each of these individually or negotiate them individually, you’re talking about more legal fees for outside counsel, more legal fees for the plaintiffs counsel. It’s just better all around to get these off of our plate, take care of the people who were harmed and focus on a better future for the city of Chicago.”</p><p>But Dowell warned there are more Guevara cases “in the pipeline.”</p><p>Asked how the city would find the money to pay for those additional settlements, “That’s not my question. I don’t have an answer for that.”</p><p>In a prepared statement, Johnson called the use of global settlements an "innovative approach, where warranted and appropriate, to resolve a grouping of reversed-conviction cases involving the same defendant — in a process recognizing both the importance of humane justice while safeguarding taxpayer dollars."</p><p>Ald. Bill Conway (34th), a former Cook County prosecutor who routinely opposes or closely scrutinizes settlements, said he believes the proposed settlement is a “good fiscal outcome for the people of Chicago.” </p><p>It amounts to roughly $680,000 for every year spent in prison, he said.</p><p> </p><p>“We have known in this city that we have a large and unknown liability with regard to Guevara cases specifically," Conway said. "And now, we have settled a lot of them.”</p><p>City officials say the proposed settlement is expected to save the city $300 million to $400 million in potential exposure to trial verdicts, plaintiffs' legal fees and defense costs.</p><p>Attorneys from the law firm Loevy & Loevy who represent Guevara plaintiffs would not comment Thursday.</p><p>Most of the exonerations in the Guevara cases came between 2016 and 2024, while Kim Foxx was Cook County’s state's attorney.</p><p>One man, Jacques Rivera, was exonerated in 2011 under Foxx's predecessor, Anita Alvarez. Guevara, who couldn't be reached for comment, now lives in Texas. He has never been charged with any crime.</p><p> Johnson has been under fire for his plan to borrow tens of millions of dollars and repay that money over five years to bankroll the Watts settlement and other large payouts tied to allegations of police misconduct.</p><p>For more than a year, Richardson-Lowry was under pressure take what she learned from the Watts settlement and strike a similar deal to resolve the outstanding Guevara cases.</p><p></p><p>The Watts cases were easier to settle because Watts pleaded guilty while Guevara has taken the Fifth. In addition, the Watts victims served shorter sentences for their shakedown cases and were represented by only two attorneys. Guevara’s alleged torture victims served longer sentences after being framed. Many of the witnesses have since died.</p><p></p><p></p><p>The $260.8 million price tag helps explain why the mayor said last month that projected legal settlements were the "biggest driver" of his projected $882 million budget shortfall for 2027.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sophie Sherry.</i></p>

entries.title: Labor-aligned group sees boon in jobs and tax revenues with Illinois data center growth
entries.summary: <p>Data center projects planned in Illinois over the next decade could generate tens of thousands of new jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenues but also drive up utility bills, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoisepi.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ILEPI-PMCR-Data-Centers-in-Illinois-_FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>report</u></a> released Thursday.</p><p>The state is expecting $57 billion worth of new data center projects through 2035, which the labor-backed think tank, Illinois Economic Policy Institute, and the University of Illinois say could create 121,000 mostly temporary skilled trade and construction jobs.</p><p>If those projects come to fruition, local municipalities could also see nearly $300 million more in annual property tax revenues, “reducing the tax burden on homeowners while funding schools, libraries, police and fire districts,” the report said.</p><p>But as the state expands its data center landscape, study author Frank Manzo said residents could have to pay $12 more per month in electric bills.</p><p>“The key is to install guardrails that minimize the risks while maximizing the value,” said Manzo, an economist at the Economic Policy Institute, which is aligned with the Illinois AFL-CIO. That umbrella labor organization is a supporter of data center construction.</p><p>Data centers and the growing use of artificial intelligence continue to dominate national debate, becoming a hot-button issue on the campaign trail. Gov. J.B. Pritzker, who is running for a historic third-term, has called for national guardrails, comparing AI to nuclear weapons.</p><p>Pritzker last month formed an<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/09/22/illinois-ai-cabinet-artificial-intelligence-pritzker" > Illinois AI cabinet</a> to “assess the various risks” of the technology, including the energy burden data centers will have on Illinois’ power grid.</p><p>And his administration, earlier this year, put a two-year pause on state tax incentives for data center construction.</p><p>Illinois has more than 200 operational or planned data centers, the largest one being a 795-acre site in Joliet slated to be operational by 2030. Manzo said Illinois ranks ninth in the U.S. for having the most centers per million residents, and that’s because the state is an “ideal destination” for many developers.</p><p>“We have a central location in the country. We have a cooler climate which really helps with heating costs,” Manzo said, adding the state’s stable of skilled and productive construction workers and university-educated workers are an additional draw for data center developers.</p><p>The projects planned the next 10 years will need 6.5 gigawatts of electricity, equivalent to powering 4.5 million homes. The report notes that electricity costs for both commercial and residential users will rise as more data centers materialize.</p><p>But, Manzo said, that can be mitigated.</p><p>He and the study’s authors have offered 10 state policy recommendations, which include the state barring utilities from raising rates by more than 5% per year and encouraging data centers to capture the heat emitted from the centers and sending it to neighboring homes and businesses.</p><p>The authors also recommend legislation to require data centers to come up with their own clean energy supply or enter into cost-sharing agreements with utility companies.</p><p>State Rep. Ann Williams, D-Chicago, said she was pleased to see many of these recommendations mimic what was in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=5513&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=167488&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>POWER Act,</u></a> a sweeping package aimed at regulating data centers’ use of energy and water, among other things.</p><p>Though it received overwhelming support from environmental groups and Democratic lawmakers, the plan failed to pass last spring. But Williams said conversations are still ongoing.</p><p>“Our priorities would be ensuring ratepayer protection, ensuring there's sufficient capacity on the grid, safeguarding water and other resources,” Williams said. “My mantra is and will continue to be as we continue to explore legislation: Put people first.”</p><p>Williams has held several legislative hearings on data centers and a town hall on the issue in her North Side district. She said many residents don’t have a positive opinion of data centers in general, and it’s not just because their utility bills are high. She said constituents also worry about the centers’ water usage and noise pollution.</p><p>“I think we're at the point with data centers that we need to mandate some of these requirements,” Williams said. “Resources don't seem to be an issue. I don't see the need for incentives, and I'm hopeful that we can avoid that conversation and really talk about what data centers can do for communities if they do locate there.”</p>

entries.title: Son of Applebee's restaurant tycoon gets prison after he 'dodged, bobbed and weaved' $1M in child support
entries.summary: <p>The son of an Applebee’s restaurant mogul was sentenced Thursday in Chicago to two years in federal prison — the maximum possible punishment under a rarely used law targeting parents who dodge paying child support.</p><p>The sentence came after Evan Musikantow, 60, was convicted last year of failing for almost two decades to pay support to his ex-wife for their two children, who grew up in the Chicago area. </p><p>Prosecutors say Musikantow, who lives in Arizona, owes about $1 million — more than half of that in interest — that he must pay his ex-wife. The unpaid support goes back to 2008, records show.</p><p>U.S. District Judge John Tharp Jr. said he was appalled when he learned Musikantow went to a casino in 2014 and bet $11,000, winning another $3,000. But not a penny went to his kids, Tharp said.</p><p>"You effectively abandoned those kids after bringing them into the world," the judge told Musikantow.</p><p>If the law allowed it, Tharp said, he would have given him even more time in prison.</p><p>"This is not conduct that the justice system ignores," Tharp said.</p><p>Musikantow’s long-running legal troubles began in the Cook County court system, where, in 2016, a judge found him in contempt of court in his 2003 divorce case. That judge told him that he had “flagrantly ignored his obligation to pay child support” and that only jail time would get his attention.</p><p>But Musikantow, who lives in Scottsdale, Arizona, with his second wife and their children, never served the six-month jail sentence imposed by the Cook County judge. That sentence was put on hold because of the federal case.</p><p>At the time, Musikantow was on Illinois’ now-defunct “Deadbeats Most Wanted List,” which named 100 parents who owed at least $5,000 in overdue support.</p><p>In 2018, federal prosecutors added to Musikantow's legal troubles, charging him under the Deadbeat Parents Punishment Act, a seldom-used law aimed at parents who cross state lines to avoid paying court-ordered support.</p><p>The next year, he went to prison for drunken driving in Arizona.</p><p>Recently, Musikantow, who has a job assembling furniture, persuaded Tharp to have the government pick up the tab for his travel from Arizona to Chicago for sentencing, telling officials he's indigent. </p><p>On Thursday, he arrived in court a free man. But he was immediately locked up after the sentencing.</p><p>Prosecutors said Musikantow's claim that he was broke didn't square with his finances. They pointed to a 2022 federal tax return listing $231,000 in gross income and also to a four-bedroom Scottsdale home he bought in 2023 for $660,000 and a Mercedes purchased the following year.</p><p>Musikantow's lawyers said the house and the car belong to his second wife.</p><p>"They are living off her money," defense attorney Mina Zardkoohi said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/08/22/deadbeat-dad-federal-prosecutors-applebees-evan-musikantow" >Musikantow told the Chicago Sun-Times last year</a> that the federal prosecution was “outrageously unfair.”</p><p>But he struck a contrite note Thursday, apologizing for his crime.</p><p>"This experience has deeply humbled me," Musikantow told the judge.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/08/22/deadbeat-dad-federal-prosecutors-applebees-evan-musikantow" target="_blank" >Musikantow blames his financial problems on a Chicago law firm </a>that handled a trust involving what he said was his 20% share of the 2001 sale of his father’s restaurant company.</p><p>Musikantow said he never received money he was owed. He sued his father and the law firm in 2015, but the case was dismissed.</p><p>His father, Allen Musikantow, testified last year that he gave his son about $1 million around 2002 — and owed him nothing more.</p><p>In a court filing, prosecutors said the trial showed that Evan Musikantow “was a college-educated, business-experienced, able-bodied defendant who dodged, bobbed and weaved his way around multiple court orders and findings of contempt year after year."</p><p>On Thursday, Assistant U.S. Attorney Edward Kohler asked the judge to throw the book at Musikantow.</p><p>"There has to be a message sent to the community that, folks, you gotta pay child support," Kohler said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/08/22/deadbeat-dad-federal-prosecutors-applebees-evan-musikantow" >Son of Applebee’s restaurant tycoon is a deadbeat dad, feds say. Evan Musikantow says he’s a victim.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/09/deadbeat-dad-tycoon-applebees-restaurant-convicted-federal-court-evan-musikantow" >Son of Applebee’s restaurant mogul convicted under federal Deadbeat Parents Punishment Act</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/8/24/18413981/son-of-applebee-s-franchise-mogul-charged-with-being-a-758-350-deadbeat-dad" >Son of Applebee’s franchise mogul charged with being a $758,350 deadbeat dad</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visits Illinois again for more Bears stadium talks with Gov. JB Pritzker
entries.summary: <p>Illinois is still moving the chains in stadium talks to keep the Bears from jumping the state line to Indiana, officials said Thursday.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker met with NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, Bears minority owner Pat Ryan and the top legislative leaders who have been wrangling for several years over the property tax incentives the team is seeking to break ground in Arlington Heights.</p><p>It was Goodell’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/14/bears-stadium-hammond-arlington-heights-report-roger-goodell-met-illinois-lawmakers-nfl-commissioner" target="_blank" ><u>second meeting</u></a> in as many months with Illinois officials, while Ryan — who bankrolled his namesake stadium opening later this week at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/10/01/northwestern-ryan-field-penn-state-wildcats-nittany-lions-evanston-friday-college-football" target="_blank" ><u>Northwestern University</u></a> — takes a more active role in negotiations with the state over Bears president Kevin Warren, who hasn’t made inroads in Springfield.</p><p>The conversation, held in Chicago, also included Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch and the Capitol’s top stadium negotiators, South Side state Sen. Bill Cunningham and downtown state Rep. Kam Buckner.</p><p>Pritzker’s office noted they’ve “remained in conversation with the Bears about their plans in Illinois throughout the summer,” since the team announced in June that they were shifting focus to Hammond, Indiana.</p><p>Sources familiar with Thursday’s discussion suggested there was no major breakthrough, but some optimism that common ground could be found before lawmakers return to Springfield in mid-November for the fall veto session. Further meetings are expected this month.</p><p>"The Governor and General Assembly leadership were glad to participate in a productive meeting focused on keeping the Bears in Illinois and protecting taxpayers,” Pritzker’s office said in a press release announcing the meeting.</p><p>"The NFL appreciated the opportunity to meet with Gov. Pritzker and legislative leaders today,” NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy said in a statement. “Timely action is essential as the Bears work to find a long-term stadium solution for the club and their fans."</p><p>A Bears spokesman didn’t reply to a request for comment.</p><p>Hoosier lawmakers have rolled out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/26/bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-hammong-senate-passes-bill-27-arlington-heights-george-mccaaskey-kevin-warren-nfl" target="_blank" ><u>the red carpet</u></a> for the Bears with legislation that would pump upwards of a billion taxpayer dollars into a new stadium.</p><p>Earlier this year, the Illinois House passed a bill that would allow the Bears to negotiate a discounted payment in lieu of taxes with local taxing bodies, earning critical support from Chicago Democrats because it would’ve shared proceeds with homeowners as property tax rebates — but those returns were deemed “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" target="_blank" ><u>negligible</u></a>.”</p><p>The Illinois Senate passed a separate bill that would allow municipalities to create their own stadium authorities to negotiate with teams, but it crumbled in the waning hours of spring session <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>without a vote in the other chamber</u></a>.</p><p>The Bears turned their noses at both measures, but haven’t spelled out what they want from the state beyond “property tax certainty.”</p><p>Ryan, a billionaire with a 10% stake in the team, has helped improve the tenor of discussions that had stagnated between Illinois officials and Halas Hall, according to sources familiar with the talks.</p><p>Goodell has toured the potential stadium sites in Arlington Heights and Hammond. Without stating a preference, he has publicly urged the Bears to come to a resolution “soon” — but Illinois sources are taking his visits as an indication that the league thinks the team is better off in its original state.</p><p>The Bears have committed to putting $2 billion into a new stadium wherever they end up. They’re under lease at Soldier Field until 2033.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sun-Times sports reporter Pat Finley</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago parking rate hikes should be tied to inflation, and out-of-towners should pay more, Ald. Dowell says
entries.summary: <p>Chicago parking rates have been frozen since 2022 and it “makes sense” to raise them annually to match the inflation rate — while asking out-of-town motorists to pay even more, the City Council’s most powerful member said Thursday.</p><p>The City Council just reached a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/29/city-council-parking-meters-deal-compromise-stonepeak-partners" > compromise deal with Stonepeak Partners,</a> the new owners of the city's parking meters, that included securing for city coffers 5% of net profits earned by Stonepeak. On the heels of that deal, Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) said Thursday that city employee pension funds stand to benefit from an automatic escalator locking in smaller, predictable parking rate increases to avoid periodic spikes.</p><p>Former Mayor Lori Lightfoot imposed an automatic escalator tying annual property tax increases to the inflation rate — before forfeiting that increase during what turned out to be her failed 2023 re-election bid. Mayor Brandon Johnson did the same.</p><p>“We haven’t raised parking rates since 2022… It makes sense to do an escalator… Making it more predictable helps everybody…Anytime we can take some revenue and put it in a lockbox and put it towards our pension liabilities, we should do that,” Dowell said.</p><p>“It may [also] be time to look at… different rates between Chicago residents — giving them a break — and charging suburbanites who use our parking system more… Suburbanites put wear and tear on our streets and use our system, and they don’t pay anything towards that.”</p><p>Dowell said there was initial talk of making future parking rate increases part of the profit-sharing compromise brokered with Stonepeak. But it was decided that “since that is a city responsibility, it did not need to be part” of the agreement. That makes setting future parking rates the next order of business for an even bigger negotiating team that Dowell has assembled.</p><p>They've already been advised that there is nothing illegal about charging different parking rates for vehicles with and without city stickers, and that separate rates would not be a violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the U.S. Constitution.</p><p>Nor does Dowell believe that charging higher parking rates for suburbanites and out-of-town motorists would discourage people from driving downtown to go to restaurants, concerts, theaters and museums, or spend the weekend in Chicago.</p><p>“People come to the city of Chicago because we have something to offer that they can’t get where they live. We have great shopping, great theater, great restaurants…They don’t come down every day. It’s a special trip,” Dowell said. “They park in garages now. They should be able to park at our meters as well."</p><p>Establishing two different sets of parking rates would require surveillance cameras and license plate readers to identify out of town vehicles.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson was kept the City Council in the dark while submitting multiple bids for the city to take back the parking meters. After dropping out, Johnson threw the entire controversy into the City Council’s lap. </p><p>Dowell said the mayor’s decision to shift from playing hide the ball to hot potato “didn’t sit well” with her colleagues and only exacerbated Johnson's already tense relationship with an emboldened City Council that she believes is on another collision course with Johnson on the pre-election city budget.</p><p>Even worse, she said, was Johnson’s decision to insinuate that the 32 City Council members who voted to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/29/city-council-raises-debt-threshold-marty-quinn-mayor-brandon-johnson" >raise City Hall’s debt threshold</a> and make it more difficult for the city to borrow money had racial motives.</p><p>“I can’t believe that Chicago has gotten to this point where we are pitting one group of people against another group of people. I don’t think that’s necessary and it’s certainly not productive,” said Dowell, one of a handful of African-American alderpersons to support what she called an exercise in “fiscal restraint.”</p><p>“We’re being divisive in our dialogue and in our politics, and we need to figure out ways to be more collaborative, to bring people together to have conversations. I don’t see that happening. That’s a problem.”</p><p>Four years ago, Dowell gave Johnson an early endorsement that turned out to be a turning point. She has since broken with the mayor, before joining the 29-member coalition that rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax.</p><p>On Thursday, Dowell was asked why she believes Johnson has had a difficult time getting along with the City Council, and has struggled with personnel issues.</p><p>“The people around him are smart people. [But] I would like to see people who have… a deeper understanding of government, who are willing to come outside of their bubble to engage with those who may not be in their bubble to work on problems,” she said. “There is a vacuum there.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-970000" name="html-embed-module-970000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_9175d23f-a7f8-4910-88a1-794bb36943ea&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml " style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Previewing Week 7's top high school football games
entries.summary: <p>It’s a loaded weekend around the area in Week 7. Here are previews of a few of the best games.</p><h3><b>No. 15 St. Ignatius at No. 1 Loyola, 1:30 p.m. Saturday</b></h3><p>After finishing 4-5 last season, Loyola (6-0) has looked more like its old self in the first season of coach John Holecek’s second stint. A talented junior class, featuring quarterback Matthew Lee, wide receiver Jordan McKinley and running back Melo Maldonado, leads the offense. Boston College-bound senior Will Mettee is an impact player on both sides of the ball. St. Ignatius (5-1) is having a bounce-back season after missing the IHSA playoffs in 2024 and 2025. The Wolfpack also have a junior quarterback to watch in Reid Hites, who missed almost all of last season with an elbow injury.</p><h3><b>Fenwick at No. 3 Brother Rice, 7 p.m. Friday</b></h3><p>This is a matchup of defending state champs. Do-everything senior Jake Thies, an Iowa-bound defensive back and running back, had his signature game for Fenwick (4-2) in its Class 6A title victory last season against East St. Louis with 200 all-purpose yards and a pair of touchdowns. Junior Myles Hill is yet another up-and-coming dual-threat quarterback. Brother Rice (4-2) is coming off an impressive 35-24 victory against Mount Carmel in which freshman quarterback Sam Holcomb accounted for 229 total yards and four touchdowns. Brayden Parks (Notre Dame) and five-star junior Kameron McGee lead a formidable defensive front for the reigning Class 7A champion Crusaders.</p><h3><b>No. 2 Lincoln-Way East at No. 21 Lincoln-Way Central, 7 p.m. Friday</b></h3><p>It’s hard to believe these two district rivals, located five miles from each other, haven’t played since the spring COVID season in 2021. Probably no team has exceeded preseason expectations more than Lincoln-Way East (6-0, 4-0 SouthWest Suburban), which shook off heavy graduation losses — most notably IHSA career passing-yards leader Jonas Williams — and has earned notable victories against Brother Rice, Kankakee, Homewood-Flossmoor and Sandburg. Illinois recruit Mason Halliman has been a rock on an offensive line that has paved the way for quarterback Evan LeFevour and running back Aidan Cavanaugh. Lincoln-Way Central (4-2, 2-1) has victories against Homewood-Flossmoor and Lockport, along with last-minute losses to Sacred Heart-Griffin and Sandburg.</p><h3><b>No. 19 Providence at No. 4 Mount Carmel, 7 p.m. Friday</b></h3><p>Both teams have been through some ups and downs. Providence (5-1) fired coach Tyler Plantz four weeks into the season, lost interim coach Adam Nissen’s debut 17-7 at Nazareth and bounced back to beat Fenwick 28-21 last week. Running backs Broden Mackert and Brayden McKay and quarterback Dominic Vita give the Celtics plenty of offensive options. Mount Carmel (4-2) has more Division I talent than any team in the state but lost starting quarterback Ryder Startz to injury in a season-opening loss to East St. Louis and fell 35-24 to Brother Rice last week. Quentin Burrell (Michigan) and Marshaun Thornton are the best wide receiver tandem in the state.</p><h3><b>No. 12 Batavia at Wheaton North, 7 p.m. Friday</b></h3><p>Batavia (4-2, 3-1 DuKane) is coming off an epic 56-49 loss to archrival Geneva in which quarterback Michael Vander Luitgaren (Wyoming) accounted for seven touchdowns and almost 500 total yards. He has passed for 1,801 yards and 23 touchdowns with five interceptions and has run for 402 yards and nine TDs. Darin Ashiru (Western Michigan) is Vander Luitgaren’s favorite target with 51 catches for 744 yards and seven touchdowns. Wheaton North (5-1, 3-1) hasn’t allowed more than 21 points in a game, which it did in its loss last week to Wheaton-Warrenville South. Watch seniors Adam Schilling, a tight end/linebacker, and Mac Murray, a running back.</p>

entries.title: Early voting kicks off in Chicago for 2026 midterm election
entries.summary: <p>As soon as Justin Labonte was old enough to vote, he made it a point to cast a ballot. He hasn’t missed an election since.</p><p>Labonte, 30, was among the earliest to arrive Thursday morning at the Chicago Voting Supersite, 137 S. State St. in the Loop, on the first day of early voting for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/how-to-vote-illinois-general" target="_blank" ><u>2026 general election</u></a>.</p><p>“I've never missed an election since I turned 18, and I certainly don't want this to be my first,” said Labonte of the West Elsdon neighborhood on the Southwest Side.</p><p>Early voting also began Thursday at the nearby supersite located at the Chicago Board of Elections office at 69 W. Washington St., 6th floor. Vote by mail has also begun.</p><p>For the first time, voters will elect the entire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago School Board</u></a>, including its president.</p><p>The ballot will also feature races for U.S. Senate, Congress, Illinois governor, attorney general, comptroller, treasurer and secretary of state, as well as seats in the Illinois General Assembly. Cook County voters will decide races for county board president and commissioners, while voters in the collar counties will see a range of additional local contests.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e60000" name="image-e60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a5653b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F99%2F251a5a8648068ba514df41c65a94%2Fearlyvoting-261002-04.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/39a3f39/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F99%2F251a5a8648068ba514df41c65a94%2Fearlyvoting-261002-04.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/03bc4d2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F99%2F251a5a8648068ba514df41c65a94%2Fearlyvoting-261002-04.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Signs for registration and early voting at the Chicago voter supersite at 137 S. State St. in the Loop Thursday. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p><i>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</i></p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Voter turnout for the midterm election in Chicago is usually between 48% to 52%, said Hernandez, except in 2018, when there was a 60% turnout.</p><p>Hernandez acknowledged fears in the community that federal immigration officers could be present at polling places. She said the Board of Elections is working with local, state and federal law enforcement agencies to ensure voters can vote without threats or intimidation.</p><p>“We are also very prepared to go to court if necessary to enforce federal and state laws,” said Hernandez. “We have laws that protect voters from intimidation, threats and coercion.”</p><p>For those reasons, Labonte said voting early is especially important for anyone who fears threats or intimidation could prevent them from casting a ballot on Nov. 3.</p><p>“Vote early, vote in person and do research on what's going to be on the ballot,” said Labonte.</p>

entries.title: Michael Douglas: One Helluva Ride, Live in Conversation in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The legendary star of <i>Wall Street</i>, <i>Romancing the Stone</i> and <i>Basic Instinct</i> comes to Chicago to tell the remarkable story of his life for the very first time.</p><p>A boy growing up in the shadow of a Hollywood legend. A gifted performer determined to prove he was more than a "TV actor." A first-time producer who stunned the industry by winning an Oscar at thirty-one. A fearless creative force who became one of the world's most celebrated movie stars.</p><p>Michael Douglas will share extraordinary behind-the-scenes stories from more than five decades at the heart of Hollywood. Featuring an unforgettable cast of legendary actors, directors and larger-than-life personalities, many of these stories have never been told before, and some are outrageously funny.</p><p>With characteristic candour and wit, he'll revisit the films that defined an era, the creative risks that changed his career and the partnerships behind some of cinema's most iconic moments. He'll also reflect on family, fame, reinvention and the personal challenges that shaped the man behind the screen.</p><p>Actor, producer, husband, father, friend and two-time Academy Award winner. Join Michael Douglas in Chicago for a rare evening of unforgettable stories, Hollywood glamour and the extraordinary life of a true screen legend.</p><p>Most seats include a pre-signed copy of <i>One Helluva Ride</i>, provided in partnership with Seminary Co-op Bookstores and 57th Street Books. More information and tickets at <a class="Link" href="https://howtoacademy.com/north-america-events/michael-douglas-one-helluva-ride/" target="_blank" >howtoacademy.com/north-america-events/michael-douglas-one-helluva-ride</a>.</p>
